text: A login screen answers one question: is this identity who it claims to be, right now. Continuous verification is the recognition that right now isn't good enough by itself — a session that passed every check at 9 a.m. can look very different by noon, so trust signals get re-checked throughout a session, not just accepted once at the door.

A device can lose its compliance status mid-session. A sign-in's risk score can change if the same account suddenly appears somewhere else. Access tokens have a limited lifetime by design, forcing a fresh evaluation instead of one login lasting indefinitely. None of that waits for the user to log out and back in — it happens while the session is still technically active.

This is where Conditional Access, already covered at a basic level earlier in this catalog, stops being just an MFA feature. Entra ID re-evaluates a policy's conditions on every single access attempt, not once at sign-in. Requiring MFA is verify explicitly in action. Requiring a compliant device is least privilege access in action. Treating an unfamiliar location as a trigger for re-verification is assume breach in action.

The practical difference from a one-time login is scale and timing. Every time a user's session touches a protected resource, Entra ID checks whether the policy's conditions still hold. If a device falls out of compliance mid-session, the next access attempt can be challenged or blocked without the user ever logging out and back in. That's 'never trust, always verify' actually running, continuously, in a real tenant.

A user signs in from a managed laptop — MFA satisfied, device compliant, location trusted — and access is granted. Twenty minutes later that laptop's compliance check fails. The next time that session reaches a protected resource, the device-compliance condition no longer holds, and the policy can require remediation or block the attempt, mid-session, without a new sign-in ever happening. Next up: Chapter 3, and how cloud providers actually protect data at rest.
